title: The scorecard: the 60 nonprofits paid most, and what anyone else recorded about their results
question: For each of the 60 nonprofits the City has paid most since fiscal year 2019, is there a result recorded by someone other than the organization, was there a target, and was it met?
finding: The 60 were paid $7.11 billion from fiscal year 2019 to 2026. 16 carry the verdict “independent measure, target missed” ($2.44 billion); 14 carry the verdict “independent measure, target met” ($1.95 billion); 5 carry the verdict “independent measure, no target” ($537.6 million); 15 carry the verdict “only its own reports” ($1.38 billion); 10 carry the verdict “no result on record” ($804.1 million). For 25 of the 60, paid $2.18 billion (31% of the money), no result recorded by anyone other than the organization itself was found.
how: Each organization is looked up in every provider-level result on disk recorded by someone else: Public Health contract monitoring tabled at the Health Commission (latest year; "missed" means a programme scored 1 or 2 of 4, or met under 80% of contracted objectives), the homelessness department's monitoring sentences in commission memos, beds occupied on the federal count night against the City's own occupancy target, federal building inspections and State adult day health attendance (independent, but with no City target). The organization's own claim is the largest count of people (or, failing that, of anything) on its latest tax return, picked out by text search and shown for contrast only. Where a monitor has recorded a result against the contract, that decides the verdict; the count-night occupancy decides it only when no monitor result is published. City money is taken from the Controller's nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only and leaves out other payments to the same organizations.
limits: A verdict describes what is published, not how well the organization works. "Target met" or "missed" usually rests on one programme or one count night out of everything the organization does, and the monitors are the departments that fund it. "Only its own reports" and "no result on record" mean no outside result was found on disk; departments hold results in systems that are not public, notably for children's, early-childhood, human-services, workforce and housing grants. For several organizations the latest published Public Health review covers a pandemic year, when sites were closed and objectives were widely missed. Organizations are matched by name. Federal and State clinic reports are filed by the organization and are counted as its own reports. The 60 are ranked on the Controller's nonprofit-spending table, that is, on contracted services. Ranked on every payment the City made, payments labelled as loans apart, 4 others would be among the 60 (Delta Dental Plan of California with $509.0 million, of which $343.6 million is labelled “Fiduciary-Benefit Payments; HtlhSvcFnd-City Hlth Plan Ex; Dental-Misc Employee” in the payment file; Homebridge Inc with $241.2 million, of which $234.2 million is labelled “Aid Payments; IHSS Contract Payments” in the payment file; SF New Deal with $75.1 million, of which $32.0 million is labelled “Materials & Supplies; Food” in the payment file; Union Square Business Improvmnt District with $52.9 million, of which $50.0 million is labelled “Current Liabilities; Unearned Rev and Other Liabs; Other Obligations-Agency Fund” in the payment file) in place of Central City Hospitality House; Bayview Hunters Pt Multipurpose Sr Svc; Bay Area Legal Aid; Project Open Hand. The nonprofit-spending table leaves those payment lines out, so these organizations are not scored here. Homebridge Inc and the other organizations whose City money that table lacks are therefore not ranked here.
